extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, and professionals (television journalists, newsroom managers, public relations and advertising practitioners, and media policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: A dissertation study modeling how extramedia, organizational, and within-media forces influence television news content (agenda building, frame building, and agenda cutting) using survey data and structural equation modeling. The work tests mediation paths among levels of influence and examines moderators like market size and staff size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extramedia Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential extramedia levels of influence include advertisers, public relations efforts, government and political, and interest groups. These sources (including press releases, press conferences, video news releases, and official proceedings) act as 'information subsidies' that can build agendas by providing ready-to-use material for journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine advertiser, public relations, and political pressures specifically as the three indicators of extramedia influence. Consider how information subsidies may be used verbatim or incorporated into coverage; without fact checking the media may help sources set their agendas. Examples: VNRs, press releases; citation to Gandy's 'information subsidies.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser Pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers may exert influence on news organizations because media rely on advertising revenue; influence may be subtle/indirect (e.g., advance notice to reschedule ads) or direct (economic pressure, pulling ads, specifying themes to avoid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for instances of advertisers pulling ads or demanding content restrictions (examples: Camel News Caravan, Ms. magazine and Clairol). Note claims from surveys (e.g., editors reporting advertisers tried to influence stories, attempted to kill stories, or applied economic pressure). Consider Baker/Bagdikian criticisms that media serve advertisers' interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Relations Pressure (PR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations efforts function as information subsidies that supply journalists with event-based or organization-based information (press releases, conferences, VNRs) intended to influence the news agenda and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess PR as a key extramedia indicator alongside advertising and political pressures; evaluate how reliance on PR materials (especially when understaffed) can lead journalists to report topics favored by sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/Government Pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Governmental and political actors can exert extramedia influence by attempting to shape coverage or restrict attention to certain topics or frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include political pressures as a distinct extramedia indicator in models predicting influence on coverage decisions and agenda cutting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational pressures include ownership/top-level executives, economic pressures, and staff-related pressures; organizational influences affect coverage decisions both indirectly (mediated through within-station decision-makers) and directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat organizational influences as multi-dimensional (owner/executive, economic, staff) and test both direct and mediated effects on content. Use examples (e.g., NBC/GE discomfort with SNL segment) and survey findings indicating journalists perceive corporate influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner/Executive Pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners and top-level executives can directly or indirectly influence story selection and framing; managerial displeasure or executive directives may lead to cutting or altering content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate owner/executive pressure as a distinct organizational indicator; consider anecdotal and survey evidence (e.g., journalists reporting corporate owners influence coverage 'a great deal' or 'a fair amount').

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic Organizational Pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic pressures at the organizational level (revenue concerns, advertiser dependence, bottom-line priorities) can shape news choices and priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model economic pressure separately from ownership/executive influence; consider how market competition and deregulation (e.g., Telecommunications Act) create incentives affecting content decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff-Related Organizational Pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff size and staff-related pressures within the organization (including resource limitations) influence the likelihood that external information subsidies will be used and that certain stories will be covered or cut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include staff size/pressure as an organizational indicator and potential moderator; smaller staffs may lead to greater reliance on extramedia sources and more perceived pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-Media Influences (Within-Newsroom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressures within the news organization include direct management pressures (explicit orders) and indirect management signals (subtle cues such as yawning, mockery, or not running a story) that socialize reporters into routines and shape content choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat within-media influences as the mediation pathway through which extramedia and organizational pressures affect content. Distinguish between direct instruction and subtler socialization processes when operationalizing measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Management Pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct instructions from newsroom managers to nix a story, cover it from a particular angle, or provide overt direction about content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure explicit managerial directives separately from indirect cues; consider how direct pressures manifest in newsroom policies or explicit editing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Management Signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtle management signals (yawning at a story idea, making fun of ideas, not running a reporter's piece) that lead to socialization into newsroom routines without overt reprimand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize indirect signals (examples given) as part of within-media influences; consider cumulative socialization effects on reporters' later choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gatekeeping Theory / Levels of Influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Gatekeeping: gatekeepers at successive levels select or reject news items as they move toward broadcast/publication. Shoemaker and Reese's hierarchical model identifies levels of influence (ideological, extramedia, organizational, media routines, individual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gatekeeping as the conceptual basis for modeling layered influences. Explicitly reference Shoemaker and Reese when specifying levels in theoretical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content Influence / Outcome Measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The dependent variables are instances of agenda building, frame building, and agenda cutting — i.e., what topics are chosen, how stories are framed, and which stories are not covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize outcomes as (1) levels of agenda building (what forces attempt to influence the news agenda), (2) frame building/frame setting (how stories are given an angle or spin), and (3) agenda cutting (pressure to not cover an item). Note that agenda cutting is identified as under-studied and worthy of theoretical development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda Building
rubrics_metrics.description: Agenda building concerns what forces are attempting to influence the news agenda — the selection and prominence of topics covered by the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure which external/organizational actors attempt to set the agenda and quantify their reported influence on topic choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame Building / Frame Setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame building addresses how forces attempt to influence the 'spin' or angle of a story — ultimately shaping the stance taken on an issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether extramedia or organizational actors affect the frames used in coverage, using reporters' perceptions of spin/angle influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda Cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: Agenda cutting is the process by which journalists are pressured to not cover or to avoid covering a particular story or issue; characterized as little-studied beyond anecdotal examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include agenda cutting as a distinct outcome variable; investigate its predictors (extramedia and organizational pressures) and moderators (market/staff size).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesized Mediation Structure (IOMC Model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The IOMC (Influences on Media Content) model proposes that extramedia and organizational influences on content are mediated through within-media organizational pressures; extramedia and organizational levels are modeled with reciprocal implication but no initial direct effects proposed between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test mediation paths where extramedia/organizational influences affect within-media pressures which in turn affect content outcomes. Model direct and indirect paths for organizational influences (both mediated and direct effects on content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) as Measurement/Evaluation Method
rubrics_metrics.description: An advanced multivariate statistical technique (SEM) is used to test the hypothesized model of influences and outcomes; SEM evaluates the overall model but does not assess unspecified relationships, necessitating follow-up regression and correlation analyses for specific links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SEM (measurement and structural models) to assess latent constructs and their indicators; supplement with correlation and multiple regression to probe unspecified or detailed relationships. The study uses a multi-stage approach: initial SEM model testing followed by construct/parameter assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey of Television Reporters (Data Source and Operationalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original data come from a national Web survey of television reporters; the survey instrument operationalizes latent constructs with observed variables (see Table 3.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on reporters' perceptions as primary measures of perceived pressures and influences. Document survey implementation procedures, consent, recruitment messages, and reminders (appendices provide full instrument and messages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Market Size and Staff Size as Moderators/Contextual Variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Market size affects reporters' perceptions of influences (respondents from smaller markets perceive more extramedia, organizational, and within-media pressures), and staff size is considered in analyses of pressure and influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include market size and staff size as contextual predictors or moderators when modeling perceived influence on content and agenda cutting (Tables and regression models examine these effects).
